Family Health

Salpingectomy: removing one or both fallopian tubes

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Salpingectomy removes one or both fallopian tubes. It may treat a damaged tube or an ectopic pregnancy, form part of cancer care, reduce certain cancer risks or provide permanent contraception. The reason, the amount removed and any additional operation matter. Removing a tube is not automatically the same as removing an ovary or the uterus.

Start with the exact operation and organs

Unilateral salpingectomy removes one tube; bilateral salpingectomy removes both. A partial salpingectomy removes a segment rather than the entire tube. Salpingotomy or salpingostomy is different: an opening is made in a tube, for example to remove an ectopic pregnancy while leaving the tube. Confirm which procedure is planned, because preserving a tube and removing it have different consequences.

Oophorectomy removes an ovary. Salpingo-oophorectomy removes a tube and ovary, on one or both sides. Hysterectomy removes the uterus. These operations may be combined, including with a cesarean or another pelvic operation, but are separate decisions. Ask which structures will remain and what unexpected findings could change the agreed plan.

Why might a tube need to be removed?

A tubal ectopic pregnancy, a ruptured or badly damaged tube, selected blocked or fluid-filled tubes, severe infection or tubal cancer can lead to a discussion of salpingectomy. Not every ectopic pregnancy or blocked tube requires removal. Stable, carefully selected ectopic pregnancies may be monitored or treated medically; rupture or serious internal bleeding requires emergency treatment. The other tube, fertility wishes and safety affect the surgical choice.

For a hydrosalpinx, a damaged fluid-filled tube, removal or occlusion may improve IVF outcomes in suitable patients. Some less damaged tubes may have other treatment options. Pelvic infection usually needs prompt prescribed antibiotics; an abscess may need hospital care, drainage or selected surgery. Suspected cancer needs a gynecologic oncology plan, which may involve more than tube removal. A list of possible indications cannot choose the operation for you.

Cancer prevention and permanent contraception

Some high-grade serous cancers described as ovarian cancers begin in the fallopian tube. Removing tubes can reduce risk, but does not prevent every ovarian or related cancer. ACOG’s 2026 update supports complete bilateral salpingectomy during appropriate planned operations and prefers it as the tubal procedure for people choosing permanent contraception after shared decision making. Feasibility, individual circumstances and consent still matter.

Inherited high risk, including some BRCA-related situations, needs separate genetic and specialist counseling. Tube-only removal is not an established substitute for all recommended tube-and-ovary risk-reducing surgery. NICE limits salpingectomy with delayed ovary removal for inherited-risk prevention to clinical trials. Discuss the actual variant, timing, fertility, menopause consequences and remaining risk rather than relying on a blanket percentage or prevention promise.

What happens to hormones, periods and fertility?

If the ovaries and uterus remain, tube removal does not intentionally stop ovarian hormones or periods and does not by itself cause immediate surgical menopause. Short-term ovarian-function evidence is reassuring in relevant settings, but does not guarantee every person’s long-term symptoms or menopause timing. Removing both ovaries before natural menopause has different consequences; removing the uterus prevents carrying a pregnancy.

After removal of one tube, spontaneous pregnancy can remain possible, depending on the remaining tube, age and other fertility factors. It is not guaranteed. Complete removal of both tubes is permanent and cannot be undone by reconnecting them; conception through the tubes is not expected. IVF may bypass them if the remaining reproductive organs and other factors are suitable, without guaranteeing a baby. Ask for fertility advice before planned surgery when possible.

Make the treatment decision before the procedure

Ask why removal is recommended, whether observation, medicines, drainage, repair or another approach is reasonable, and what might happen without treatment. Options differ between an emergency, infertility treatment, cancer and prevention. Share pregnancy wishes, previous operations and concerns about retaining organs. An urgent situation may limit choices, but explanations and consent remain important.

The route depends on the indication, anatomy, adhesions, health and available expertise. A planned keyhole operation may need to become an open operation if safe completion is difficult. Ask whether one or both tubes, part of a tube, or other organs could be removed and how the tissue will be examined. Cancer surgery or another combined procedure can change both the extent and recovery.

Practical preparation and anesthesia

Tell the team about all medicines, supplements, allergies, health conditions and previous anesthetic problems. Follow the exact instructions for fasting, drinking and medicines; do not stop prescribed treatment yourself. Tests are selected for the situation, and the team may need to exclude pregnancy before a planned procedure. Emergency care should not be delayed to complete a routine preparation checklist.

Laparoscopic removal usually uses general anesthesia. An operation during childbirth or another combined procedure may have a different anesthetic plan. Arrange collection, the recommended adult supervision, help with children and comfortable loose clothing. Follow restrictions on driving, machinery, alcohol and important decisions after anesthesia even if you feel awake. Tell the service if you cannot arrange support.

What the professional procedure can involve

For laparoscopy, small abdominal openings allow a camera and instruments to enter; gas creates space to see and operate. The surgeon separates and removes the agreed tube or tubes, controls bleeding and closes the openings. An open abdominal operation uses a larger incision; surgery with a cesarean may use the existing access. Ask the team to explain how your planned procedure will be carried out.

The number and size of cuts, operation length and anesthesia time vary. Previous infection, scar tissue, bleeding or an additional operation can make care more complex. Keyhole surgery often has smaller skin wounds and a shorter recovery than open surgery, but is not automatically possible or safest in every circumstance. Ask what changes to the planned approach could be needed.

The first hours and days of recovery

Staff monitor you while anesthesia wears off and treat pain or nausea. Tiredness, abdominal soreness, bruising or bloating can occur; gas-related shoulder discomfort may follow laparoscopy. Ask what should improve and which pain medicine is suitable. Symptoms must be judged by their severity and progress, not assumed harmless because surgery was recent.

Some people leave the same day; others need longer observation or treatment. Discharge depends on the operation and recovery, including a safe plan for drinking, moving, bladder function and support. Bleeding can occur after ectopic-pregnancy treatment or some combined procedures, but heavy bleeding or deterioration is not something to wait out. Keep wound-care instructions and the surgical contact details accessible.

Returning to activity takes an individual plan

Recovery may take weeks, with longer healing after a larger or more complicated operation. A fixed two-to-four-week or three-to-six-week estimate is not clearance for everyone. Small skin wounds do not show all internal healing. Start the movement advised by the team and ask separately about work, lifting, exercise, bathing, driving and sex.

Avoid forcing painful activity and arrange practical help with heavy tasks. Readiness also depends on pain treatment and any birth, infection, cancer treatment or pregnancy loss accompanying the operation. Emotional recovery may take a different amount of time from wound healing. Discuss ongoing pain, anxiety or grief rather than treating a recovery deadline as a test you must pass.

Possible complications and realistic risk discussion

Risks include infection, internal or wound bleeding, a hernia, anesthesia problems, blood clots and injury to nearby organs or blood vessels. Adhesions or previous disease can affect difficulty. Sometimes another procedure or conversion to open surgery is needed. Research in selected patients having salpingectomy with a cesarean or another planned operation cannot establish your personal risk or guarantee complication-free surgery.

Ask which risks matter for you and what prevention is planned. Use prescribed clot prevention or other medicines exactly as instructed; do not start leftover antibiotics or blood thinners yourself. New fever, chills, wound redness, swelling or discharge, urinary burning, persistent vomiting, or new pain or swelling in one leg needs urgent same-day assessment. The emergency signs below require faster action.

When to obtain immediate help

Seek immediate emergency care for severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, pain with movement or touch, heavy bleeding, faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, new confusion, chest pain or breathing difficulty. With possible pregnancy, shoulder-tip pain is also an emergency warning; do not wait for a positive test. Complete inability to pass urine needs immediate care as well, without waiting for sudden onset or severe pain.

Do not drive yourself: ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. Tell the team which operation you had and when, and bring the medicine list. An ectopic pregnancy can cause internal bleeding without obvious vaginal bleeding. Do not dismiss serious chest or shoulder symptoms as ordinary surgical gas, or delay help to take extra pain medicine, repeat a home test or finish an app entry.

Follow-up and future pregnancy planning

Clarify the operative findings, tissue results, any further treatment and follow-up before considering care complete. After salpingectomy for an ectopic pregnancy, NICE advises a urine pregnancy test after three weeks and further assessment if positive; tube-preserving surgery needs a different hormone follow-up plan. This is not a routine test schedule after removal for every other indication. Follow the treating service’s written instructions and seek care sooner for symptoms.

If one tube remains and pregnancy is not wanted, contraception is still needed. If both tubes were removed for contraception, confirm the exact procedure and transition instructions before stopping another method. Tubal surgery does not protect against STIs. If pregnancy is wanted or suspected later, mention the surgery and any previous ectopic pregnancy so location and follow-up can be assessed early. Do not dismiss a positive test or concerning pain and bleeding because a tube-removal operation took place.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the surgeon to name the exact one-sided or bilateral procedure, which organs remain, why it is recommended and what alternatives or unexpected findings could change the plan.

Keep written fasting, medicine, transport, wound-care and activity instructions. Ask about tissue results, any ectopic-pregnancy follow-up and fertility or contraception plans before leaving care.

Seek help according to symptoms rather than a recovery deadline. Keep emergency contacts available, do not drive yourself for emergency assessment and do not alter medicines or start home treatments without the team.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can organize the operation name and date, organs removed, medicines, recovery symptoms, follow-up tests and questions about fertility or prevention. It cannot choose the procedure, assess a wound or internal bleeding, diagnose ectopic pregnancy, confirm cancer prevention or predict IVF success. Recording must not delay urgent care.

When to seek help

Seek urgent same-day assessment for fever, chills, wound changes, urinary burning, persistent vomiting or new pain or swelling in one leg. Obtain immediate emergency care for severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, pain with movement or touch, heavy bleeding, faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, new confusion, chest pain or breathing difficulty. Shoulder-tip pain with possible pregnancy is another emergency warning, even without a positive test. Complete inability to urinate requires immediate care too. Do not drive yourself; arrange another driver or an ambulance. Follow the exact recovery and pregnancy-related follow-up plan; do not self-prescribe antibiotics, blood thinners or other treatments.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Tube removal, ovary removal and hysterectomy are different operations; ask exactly what will be removed.
  • The reason matters: an ectopic pregnancy, infection, blockage, cancer and prevention do not all require the same treatment.
  • Retained ovaries generally continue hormone production; one-tube pregnancy and IVF possibilities are individual, not guarantees.
  • Preparation, discharge and return to activity must fit the actual operation rather than a fixed recovery calendar.
  • Severe or worsening pain, heavy bleeding, fainting, chest or breathing symptoms and inability to urinate need immediate care.

Frequently asked questions

Which warning signs need help after salpingectomy?

Fever, wound changes, urinary burning, persistent vomiting or new pain or swelling in one leg need urgent same-day advice. Severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, pain on movement or touch, heavy bleeding, faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, new confusion, chest pain, breathing difficulty or complete inability to urinate need immediate care. Shoulder-tip pain with possible pregnancy is another emergency warning. Do not drive yourself.

What complications are possible?

Infection, bleeding, hernia, anesthesia problems, blood clots and injury to nearby organs or vessels are possible. Risk depends on your health, indication, prior disease and exact operation. Keyhole surgery may need conversion to an open operation; no small incision or study result guarantees an uncomplicated recovery.

Why is a fallopian tube removed?

Possible reasons include a tubal ectopic pregnancy, a ruptured tube, severe tubal damage or selected hydrosalpinx, infection, cancer, risk reduction or permanent contraception. These are not automatic indications in every patient. Ask about the diagnosis, suitable alternatives and the consequences of removing one or both tubes.

How does it differ from salpingo-oophorectomy?

Salpingectomy removes tube tissue. Oophorectomy removes an ovary; salpingo-oophorectomy removes a tube and ovary, on one or both sides. Hysterectomy removes the uterus. These may be combined but should be separately named, explained and agreed.

Will my periods stop or will I enter menopause?

Tube-only removal normally leaves ovarian hormone production and periods intact when the ovaries and uterus remain. Removing both ovaries before natural menopause causes surgical menopause; removing the uterus stops ordinary periods. Confirm the actual organs involved and ask about new symptoms rather than assuming every later change is due to the tubes.

Can I still become pregnant?

Pregnancy may be possible with one remaining tube, depending on its condition and other factors. Complete removal of both tubes is permanent and cannot be reconnected; IVF may be possible if otherwise suitable. Neither a remaining tube nor IVF guarantees a baby. Seek prompt advice for a suspected pregnancy after any tubal surgery.

Does removal of both tubes prevent every ovarian cancer?

No. It can reduce the risk of some cancers, but does not remove all ovarian or related cancer risk. Inherited high risk needs separate specialist advice; tube-only removal is not automatically equivalent to recommended tube-and-ovary risk-reducing surgery.

How long will recovery and follow-up take?

They depend on the reason, route, additional procedures and your progress. Get written instructions for wound care, medicines, activity and when to call. Ectopic-pregnancy treatment also needs its specific pregnancy-hormone or test follow-up. Do not wait for a routine appointment if warning signs develop.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
